lesson_title: Data Handling: from Survey Question to Honest Graph
hook_text: Nine friends. Mean spending R40. Median R35. Same data, two answers — and one of them is lying to you.
clip_script: Nine friends, weekly airtime money, sorted: 20, 25, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45, 50 — and one big spender at 90. The mean: pool it all, R360, share it out — R40 each. The median: line them up, tap the middle shoulder — R35. Why the fight? That R90. The mean shook hands with it — every rand goes in the pot, so one big spender drags the share-out up. The median never met it — the queue's middle doesn't care how rich the last person is. Outliers in the data? Trust the median. That's why the news says MEDIAN income, not mean. Now the graph trick. Two bars: R36 and R40. Start the axis at R35 and the R40 bar towers five times taller — a R4 gap dressed up as a landslide. Check where the axis starts, read the real numbers, say them out loud. And before any of it: who did you ask? Survey only your grade 11 friends and the whole school looks richer than it is. That's bias — and chance, not convenience, is the only fair chooser.
visual_style: Nine learners in a queue holding rand amounts overhead, the R90 friend glowing as the mean slides up a number line while the median stands still; a bar graph whose floor rises to R35 and back to zero, the towering bar deflating to honest size.
mood: Sceptical and empowering — the friend who teaches you to catch statistics misbehaving.
pacing: Playful through the queue and share-out, a snap of tension at the outlier, slowing to a deliberate reveal on the truncated axis.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and never be fooled by an average or a graph again.
